t: Install and first eval in minutes
title: Install and first eval in minutes
description: Promptfoo installs with `npx promptfoo@latest init` (or npm/pip), which scaffolds a promptfooconfig.yaml. `promptfoo eval` then runs every prompt against every provider and test case, printing a pass/fail table. The whole loop from zero to a scored eval is minutes, which is why teams adopt it before prompts get complicated.

demo.program:
print('npx promptfoo@latest init  # scaffold config')
print('promptfoo eval              # run scored eval')
demo.expected_output:
npx promptfoo@latest init  # scaffold config
promptfoo eval              # run scored eval

title: The eval config file
description: promptfooconfig.yaml declares prompts (inline or files), providers (model endpoints), tests (vars + assertions), and output settings. One file fully describes an eval, so it lives in git next to the prompts and runs in CI. Config-as-code is what makes prompt testing repeatable instead of vibes.

title: Providers: local and cloud models
description: Providers name the models under test: openai:, anthropic:, ollama:, huggingface:, azure:, bedrock:, and dozens more, each with model and parameter options. The same eval runs unchanged against a local Ollama model or a cloud API by swapping the provider string. Local-first testing keeps iteration free and private.

title: Assertions: how outputs are scored
description: Assertions score each output: equals, contains, icontains, regex, llm-rubric (an LLM judge with a rubric), cost/latency thresholds, and custom Python/JS functions. An eval is only as good as its assertions; llm-rubric handles fuzzy quality while deterministic checks handle format. Thresholds turn quality bars into numbers.

title: Test cases from CSV
description: Test vars can live in a CSV (one row per case), so non-engineers add cases in a spreadsheet and the eval picks them up. Columns map to prompt variables; expected outputs can ride in an __expected column. This is how prompt test suites grow to hundreds of cases without YAML sprawl.

print('tests.csv: one row per case, columns = prompt vars')
print('__expected column holds gold outputs')

__expected column holds gold outputs

title: Web viewer for results
description: `promptfoo view` opens a local web UI showing every prompt x test result, diffs between runs, and failure drill-downs. Comparing two eval runs side by side shows exactly which cases a prompt change fixed or broke. The viewer is what makes eval results legible to the whole team.

title: Red teaming plugin
description: promptfoo redteam generates adversarial attacks (jailbreaks, prompt injection, PII leaks, harmful content elicitation) against your prompts and scores the defenses. Strategies include Crescendo, GOAT, and injection variants. It turns 'hope the prompt is safe' into a measured attack battery.

print('promptfoo redteam run  # adversarial battery')
print('strategies: jailbreak, injection, PII, harmful')

title: CI integration
description: Evals run in CI with `promptfoo eval --no-cache`, failing the build when pass rates drop below a threshold (--threshold). Cached results speed up local reruns. Prompt changes become pull requests with eval scores attached, like unit tests for language.

demo.program: print('promptfoo eval --threshold 0.95  # fail CI below bar')
demo.expected_output: promptfoo eval --threshold 0.95  # fail CI below bar

title: Prompt file organization
description: Prompts live as separate files (prompt1.txt, prompt2.md) referenced from the config, so prompt engineering is file editing with history, not strings buried in code. Variants are files too, making prompt A/B a config change. Organization scales because prompts are assets.

title: Model-graded evals done right
description: llm-rubric assertions use a judge model with an explicit rubric and pass threshold, and promptfoo supports multiple judges and majority vote to reduce judge bias. Rubrics are versioned with the eval. Judge-based scoring is powerful but only trustworthy with rubrics and redundancy.

title: Latency and cost tracking
description: Every eval records per-provider latency and token cost, so choosing between models is a data question: quality score vs ms vs dollars. The web viewer charts these tradeoffs. Cost-aware model selection starts with measured numbers.

description: `promptfoo share` uploads an eval run to a shareable link for review without exposing keys. Teammates see the full result table and diffs. Sharing makes prompt review async and concrete.

title: Custom providers and assertions
description: Any HTTP endpoint or local script can be a provider via exec: or custom JS/Python hooks, and assertions can be arbitrary functions. This escapes the built-in list: in-house models and domain-specific scorers plug in cleanly. Extensibility is why promptfoo fits odd stacks.

demo.program: print('provider: exec:./my-model.sh  # anything is a provider')
demo.expected_output: provider: exec:./my-model.sh  # anything is a provider

title: Dataset and conversation evals
description: Multi-turn evals script conversations (user turns + expected assistant behavior per turn), and datasets pin regression cases. Conversation evals catch the failures single-turn tests miss: context loss, tone drift, premature answers. Real chat products need both.

title: Guardrail testing patterns
description: Teams encode guardrails as assertions (no PII, no disallowed content, citation present) and run them on every prompt change. The redteam plugin then attacks the same guardrails. Defense in depth: assertions for the known rules, red teams for the unknown attacks.

demo.program: print('guardrails = assertions + redteam attacks, every change')
demo.expected_output: guardrails = assertions + redteam attacks, every change
